title: The teacher nearby
hook: the most important teacher may be at a local temple

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Therigatha, Soma under her tree, and women leading in the halls today. Your line: they lead.

A row of shoes by a door in a strip mall, between a laundromat and a tax office. Inside, a small room: a Buddha on a shelf, cushions, a kettle, and a monk or a lay teacher who's been there every week for years, sitting with whoever turns up. No livestream, no book tour. For weeks now, this path has walked with famous names: Dogen, Hakuin, Ajahn Chah, the Dalai Lama. Today turns toward the door you may have walked past without noticing.
screen: `SHOES BY A STRIP-MALL DOOR.` → `FAMOUS NAMES FOR WEEKS.` → `NOW, THE DOOR NEARBY.`

segments.voice: There's a short exchange in the Pali Canon. Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, comes to him with a thought he's been turning over. Admirable friendship, he says, having good companions on the path, must be half of the holy life. The Buddha corrects him. Don't say that, Ananda. Admirable friendship is the whole of the holy life. The Pali word is kalyanamitta, a lovely friend, a good friend in the dharma. Notice the kind of teacher this points to. Not someone you admire from far away. A friend: someone who knows your face, sees you on a bad week, notices when you stop coming. Books and recorded talks can teach a great deal, and famous teachers have real gifts. But a book can't see you slump on the cushion. A recording can't ask how your mother is doing. The person at the local temple or sitting group can. Where Buddhism is old, the local temple can be where people learn: the monk down the road who chants at a funeral, teaches children, listens to a farmer's worry. Elsewhere, the nearby teacher might be a lay volunteer who opens a room on Tuesday nights. Traditions differ in how they choose and train teachers, and some places nearby will suit you better than others. That's fine. The point of the old exchange is simple: the path is walked with people, and the ones who can walk it with you are close enough to know you. Some readers take a plain lesson from it: look first for the good friend nearby.
screen: `HALF THE HOLY LIFE? NO, THE WHOLE.` · `KALYANAMITTA: A GOOD FRIEND.` · `A BOOK CAN'T SEE YOU SLUMP.` · `THE TEMPLE DOWN THE ROAD.` · then, large: `CLOSE ENOUGH TO KNOW YOU.`

segments.voice: Picture the streets around where you live, slowly, as if you were walking them: is there a temple, a meditation group, a quiet room where people sit together? You may not know, and that's fine; just notice the not knowing. Then remember someone close by who has already been a good friend to your practice, even without the title of teacher, and let a little thanks go toward them.
Kalyanamitta. The good friend close enough to know you, whom the Buddha called the whole of the holy life.
Your line: nearby. Good friendship is the whole of the path, not half. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhists in Asia often learn at the neighborhood temple, where resident monks or nuns teach and lead ceremonies; elsewhere, local sitting groups led by monastics or trained lay teachers meet weekly and welcome newcomers.

options: no, it's the whole of the holy life
fork.reveal: the Buddha says don't say that: admirable friendship is the whole of the holy life.

original.note: Pali kalyanamitta: a lovely friend, a good friend on the path.

trapdoor: what you thought: a real teacher has to be famous.
what it means: the good friend close enough to know you is, the Buddha says, the whole of the holy life.
what a scholar hears: the Upaddha Sutta's kalyanamittata, admirable friendship, as the ground of the path.

chat.says: Can't I just learn Buddhism from podcasts and books instead of a local group?
options: They help, but the Buddha called good friendship the whole of the holy life.
No, books and recordings are forbidden; only a robed monk may teach you.
Sure, Ananda's point was that friends are half the path; books cover the rest.
chat.meaning: Ananda said admirable friendship is half the holy life; the Buddha said it's the whole. A book can't see you slump; a good friend nearby can.
